When to Trust Simulated Patient Responses:
Support-Gated World Models for Vasopressor Decision Support

Yifan Jin Affiliation: Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou, Guangdong, China    Tao Liu Affiliation: Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou, Guangdong, China
Abstract

Clinical world models expose language-model agents to predicted patient responses, but simulations can be unreliable for poorly supported treatments or unfamiliar hospitals. We introduce Support-Gated World-Model decision support (SG-WM), a lightweight extension of a propose–simulate–refine agent. A recurrent dynamics ensemble predicts short-horizon physiological responses to documented norepinephrine dose categories, while a behavior model estimates observational action support. The interface withholds predictions with insufficient support or excessive ensemble disagreement and abstains when no candidate qualifies. Evaluation on eICU-CRD includes 70 hospitals and 30,700 decision transitions, with 14 hospitals held out for testing. At 62.0% factual-transition coverage, joint gating yields a MAP mean absolute error of 7.3 mmHg, compared with 9.2 mmHg for random selection at the same coverage. The gated agent achieves 60.0% agreement with recorded actions at 81.0% decision coverage, compared with 55.0% agreement and 99.5% coverage for an ungated ensemble agent. Component ablations show lower factual risk with joint gating than with either gate alone. These results characterize a reliability–coverage trade-off in selective clinical simulation; they do not identify individualized treatment effects or establish improved patient outcomes.

1 Introduction

World-model-augmented clinical agents connect a decision model to learned patient dynamics. SepsisAgent combines treatment proposals, simulated responses, and refinement, with additional agent training (Wu et al., 2026). medDreamer uses imagined latent trajectories for clinical policy learning (Xu et al., 2025). These studies motivate asking how a decision agent should use a simulator whose reliability varies across patients and actions.

An observational simulator has uneven data support. A candidate dose may be uncommon for a particular history, and a new hospital may differ in case mix, treatment documentation, and monitoring. An agent that receives all predictions in the same format can mistake model confidence for clinical evidence. Predictive accuracy under the recorded action also does not establish the correctness of an unobserved treatment alternative. These problems motivate a narrower question than autonomous treatment optimization: can a small interface change reduce reliance on unreliable simulated responses, while making its coverage cost measurable?

We propose SG-WM, which retains a recurrent clinical dynamics model and a propose–simulate–refine agent, but adds a candidate-level support and disagreement gate. Only eligible predictions are released to the agent. Rejected candidates receive explicit reason codes; an empty eligible set produces abstention. We evaluate the framework on eICU-CRD, whose multi-hospital structure enables testing on unseen sites (Pollard et al., 2018). The evaluation separates factual predictive reliability from the behavior of the simulation-augmented agent.

The study makes three contributions: (1) a precise interface separating supported predictions, withheld predictions, and abstention; (2) a hospital-held-out evaluation that measures predictive error and coverage together; and (3) a matched ensemble baseline and component ablations that isolate the effects of support restriction and model disagreement. On held-out hospitals, joint gating reduces factual prediction error relative to matched random selection, while making the associated reduction in decision coverage explicit.

2 Related work and positioning

Clinical world models.

Generative models of longitudinal health records provide important foundations for modeling patient trajectories. Foresight forecasts future medical events from electronic health records, while Delphi-2M models disease trajectories at population scale (Kraljevic et al., 2024; Shmatko et al., 2025). In medical imaging, MedDream learns a shared latent radiographic state that supports diagnostic reasoning and report-conditioned image generation, extending world-model formulations to the interpretation and synthesis of clinical imaging evidence (Xi et al., 2026b). Intervention-oriented approaches further incorporate treatment actions into patient-state prediction. Medical World Model explores treatment-conditioned tumor simulation, and EHRWorld addresses long-horizon clinical trajectory simulation under sequential interventions (Yang et al., 2025b; Mu et al., 2026). Meanwhile, medDreamer and SepsisAgent integrate learned patient dynamics into policy learning and language-agent interaction, respectively (Xu et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026). Complementary medical vision-language research examines how clinical language can be grounded in visual representations. Report-guided segmentation translates radiology findings into spatially localized image evidence (Xi et al., 2026a), while pathology vision-language pre-training combines cross-modal alignment with self-supervised learning to strengthen visual representations (Yang et al., 2025a).

Uncertainty and conservative offline learning.

Deep ensembles offer a practical approach to predictive uncertainty estimation (Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017), while evaluations under dataset shift demonstrate the importance of assessing uncertainty beyond the training distribution (Ovadia et al., 2019). In model-based offline reinforcement learning, MOPO and MOReL address model exploitation through uncertainty penalties and pessimistic environment models (Yu et al., 2020; Kidambi et al., 2020). Related approaches address distributional shift through conservative value estimation, as in Conservative Q-Learning, or restrict deviations from a baseline policy in poorly supported regions, as in SPIBB (Kumar et al., 2020; Laroche et al., 2019). Selective prediction provides a complementary perspective: SelectiveNet explicitly studies the trade-off between predictive risk and coverage through a reject option (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2019). Our method brings these perspectives to an LLM-facing clinical simulation interface, combining candidate-level support filtering, disagreement-based rejection, and explicit abstention.

Clinical interpretation.

Evaluating treatment recommendations from observational healthcare data requires separating predictive performance from policy quality and clinical benefit (Gottesman et al., 2019). Counterfactual off-policy evaluation using structural causal models provides one framework for examining how alternative policies might change individual trajectories under explicit modeling assumptions (Oberst and Sontag, 2019). In our setting, clinician agreement measures correspondence with recorded actions rather than treatment optimality, and historical action frequency represents observational support rather than a clinical safety guarantee. We therefore evaluate factual prediction error, decision coverage, and unsupported selections separately. These retrospective measures characterize the behavior of the simulation interface; establishing patient benefit requires additional causal and clinical validation.

3 Study setting and data protocol

3.1 Cohort

We study adult ICU stays with documented norepinephrine exposure in eICU-CRD v2.0 (Pollard et al., 2019). The analysis includes 8,650 patients, 9,010 eligible ICU stays, and 30,700 decision transitions across 70 hospitals. The training, validation, and test partitions contain 42, 14, and 14 hospitals, respectively, and have no hospitals in common. Table 1 summarizes cohort characteristics and dose-record exclusions. The cohort is defined by documented norepinephrine exposure rather than a Sepsis-3 diagnosis.

Interpretable dose records and pre-decision physiological history define the modeling inputs. The infusion table contains heterogeneous charted rates; missing concentration can prevent conversion from volumetric to drug dose (MIT Laboratory for Computational Physiology, n.d.a). Unresolvable dose records are excluded, and missing infusion records are distinguished from explicit zero rates. The test partition includes 70 documented zero-dose transitions. Missing MAP targets increase from 9.4% in training to 11.0% in testing.

3.2 Time alignment and treatment representation

The decision grid uses four-hour intervals within the first 72 hours after the first norepinephrine administration record satisfying the inclusion criteria. For each boundary tt, history HtH_{t} uses only entries available before tt. The index treatment ata_{t} is the first valid documented norepinephrine rate in (t,t+30 min](t,t+30\text{ min}]. The primary response Yt+1Y_{t+1} comprises mean arterial pressure (MAP) and heart rate summarized over (t+3 h,t+4 h](t+3\text{ h},t+4\text{ h}], with prespecified measurement requirements. This is an index-dose-associated prediction task: the dose is not assumed constant throughout the four-hour interval. Subsequent treatments and co-interventions remain potential confounders.

Rates are harmonized to μ\mug/kg/min only when dose units and any necessary patient weight or drug concentration are verified. The action set consists of five discrete categories: an explicit documented zero-dose category and four positive-dose intervals defined by the training-set positive-dose quartiles. The cutpoints are Q25=0.05Q_{25}=0.05, Q50=0.10Q_{50}=0.10, and Q75=0.20Q_{75}=0.20 μ\mug/kg/min. Unsupported or unresolvable records are excluded. These training-derived cutpoints remain fixed during validation and testing.

History includes prior vital-sign summaries, last available laboratory values, measurement ages, missingness indicators, verified previous medication and treatment records, and static covariates. Discharge information, future measurements, completed first-day severity summaries, and future treatment summaries are prohibited as decision inputs. Lab availability is handled conservatively using documented result/revision offsets (MIT Laboratory for Computational Physiology, n.d.b).

3.3 Hospital-held-out evaluation

The hospital split comprises 42 training sites, 14 validation sites, and 14 test sites, corresponding to a 60/20/20 partition. The test set contains 1,800 unique patients and 6,300 decision transitions. Feature scaling, dose-bin cutpoints, model fitting, and interface thresholds are development operations; test hospitals serve only for evaluation. This split examines transport to hospitals excluded from training rather than within-hospital patient interpolation.

4 Support-gated simulation interface

4.1 Shared recurrent dynamics ensemble

For a patient history HtH_{t}, a two-layer GRU produces a hidden representation hth_{t}. A candidate action is embedded and concatenated to hth_{t} before prediction. The recurrent backbone provides a lightweight history-aware representation for the action-conditioned prediction head. Each of M=3M=3 independently initialized models is trained on a patient-bootstrap sample. Every GRU has 128 hidden units and dropout of 0.1:

pθm​(Yt+1∣Ht,at)=∏j=1d𝒩⁡(Yt+1,j,μm​j​(Ht,at),σm​j2​(Ht,at)).p_{\theta_{m}}(Y_{t+1}\mid H_{t},a_{t})=\prod_{j=1}^{d}\mathcal{N}\bigl(Y_{t+1,j};\mu_{mj}(H_{t},a_{t}),\sigma^{2}_{mj}(H_{t},a_{t})\bigr). (1)

Training minimizes Gaussian negative log likelihood on observed targets only. Missing targets are masked rather than imputed as outcomes. Each member is optimized using AdamW with a learning rate of 10−310^{-3}, batch size 128, and at most 100 epochs; early stopping uses a patience of 10 epochs. The prespecified random seeds for stability assessment are 13, 42, and 2026. Predictors use training-derived scaling, and evaluation metrics are also reported in physical units where applicable.

The ensemble mean and disagreement score are

μ¯j​(H,a)\displaystyle\bar{\mu}_{j}(H,a) =1M​∑m=1Mμm​j​(H,a),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\mu_{mj}(H,a), (2)
u⁡(H,a)\displaystyle u(H,a) =1d​∑j=1d1M​∑m=1M[μm​j​(H,a)−μ¯j​(H,a)]2sj2+ϵ,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\frac{\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}[\mu_{mj}(H,a)-\bar{\mu}_{j}(H,a)]^{2}}{s_{j}^{2}+\epsilon}, (3)

where sjs_{j} is the training-set target standard deviation. Disagreement is a heuristic signal of model instability; it is not a complete estimate of epistemic uncertainty or counterfactual error. Total predictive variance additionally includes the average within-model variance. Any interval rescaling is fitted only on calibration sites. No distribution-free coverage guarantee is claimed across hospitals.

4.2 Observational action support

A separately trained GRU classifier estimates bϕ​(a∣H)b_{\phi}(a\mid H) from training histories and recorded actions. It is optimized with cross-entropy; its output probabilities are evaluated and used for support-threshold calibration on the validation hospitals. Its probabilities operationalize local observational support:

q⁡(H,a)=bϕ​(a∣H).q(H,a)=b_{\phi}(a\mid H). (4)

Low qq can indicate extrapolation risk, but high qq does not establish safety, clinical appropriateness, or exchangeability. The classifier shares the feature schema, not the fitted parameters, with the dynamics ensemble.

4.3 Candidate gate and abstention

The agent proposes up to three distinct action-bin identifiers from the predefined action set. For each candidate, the interface computes

G(H,a)=𝕀{q(H,a)≥η}𝕀{u(H,a)≤τ}.G(H,a)=\mathbb{I}\{q(H,a)\geq\eta\}\mathbb{I}\{u(H,a)\leq\tau\}. (5)

The support threshold η\eta and disagreement threshold τ\tau define the acceptance region. Starting from η0=0.05\eta_{0}=0.05 and τ0=0.03\tau_{0}=0.03, validation-set quantile calibration and grid search select the final thresholds η∗=0.06\eta^{*}=0.06 and τ∗=0.025\tau^{*}=0.025. Calibration uses recorded actions from the validation partition; the selected thresholds remain fixed throughout test-hospital evaluation. These are statistical interface thresholds rather than clinical risk limits.

When G=1G=1, the tool returns the mean response, predictive spread, disagreement score, and support score. When G=0G=0, it withholds the numerical prediction and returns LOW_SUPPORT, HIGH_DISAGREEMENT, or both. The language-model agent may select only a candidate with G=1G=1; a deterministic validator enforces this restriction. It abstains if no candidate qualifies. Uncertainty feedback and enforcement are distinct mechanisms.

4.4 Proposal and refinement configuration

We use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct for the proposal and refinement stages. Decoding is deterministic, with temperature 0, top-pp 1.0, and a maximum output length of 256 tokens per generation. At most three distinct candidate dose categories are proposed at each decision point. Responses follow a structured JSON schema containing action-category identifiers. A single repair attempt is permitted after a malformed response; another parsing failure results in invalid-output abstention. The deterministic validator checks the final category against the eligible set and rejects any selection that violates the support or disagreement constraints. The configuration and threshold-selection protocol are summarized in Appendix A.

4.5 Matched baseline and scope of adaptation

The principal comparator is an ensemble world-model agent without gating. It uses the same patient histories, candidate proposals, dynamics ensemble, LLM checkpoint, tool budget, and response summaries. It receives predictions for all proposed candidates and selects one without hard support/disagreement filtering. Matching ensemble size prevents attributing an ensembling benefit to the gate.

The comparator is a SepsisAgent-inspired inference baseline using the same proposal–simulation–refinement structure. The comparison isolates the inference interface rather than the source paper’s complete three-stage agent-training pipeline.

5 Experimental evaluation

5.1 Comparators and evaluation scope

We compare a behavior-cloning classifier, a direct LLM without simulation, an ungated ensemble world-model agent, and SG-WM. The ungated and gated agents share the dynamics ensemble and candidate-generation structure. The principal comparison therefore concerns access to candidate-level simulation feedback. Calls per case summarize average inference usage.

The evaluation separates two units of analysis. Factual prediction assesses a simulator under the action recorded in the data. Agent evaluation assesses whether a candidate set produces a non-abstaining output and which action category is selected. A factual transition may fail the gate while the agent still has another eligible candidate. Consequently, factual coverage and agent decision coverage have different denominators.

5.2 Factual prediction metrics

For a recorded action, normalized absolute prediction error is

ei=1|Oi|​∑j∈Oi|Yi​j−μ¯j​(Hi,ai)|sj+ϵ,e_{i}=\frac{1}{|O_{i}|}\sum_{j\in O_{i}}\frac{|Y_{ij}-\bar{\mu}_{j}(H_{i},a_{i})|}{s_{j}+\epsilon}, (6)

where OiO_{i} indexes observed target dimensions and sjs_{j} is the training-set standard deviation of target jj. For accepted factual transitions A={i:G⁡(Hi,ai)=1}A=\{i:G(H_{i},a_{i})=1\},

Coverage=|A|N,Risk=1|A|​∑i∈Aei.\operatorname{Coverage}=\frac{|A|}{N},\qquad\operatorname{Risk}=\frac{1}{|A|}\sum_{i\in A}e_{i}. (7)

Physical-unit MAP and heart-rate MAE provide interpretable measures of predictive error. Prediction-interval (PI) coverage measures the proportion of observed targets contained in the nominal 90% interval. The joint gate is compared with support-only selection, disagreement-only selection, and random selection at the same factual coverage. Metrics are evaluated only where the corresponding target is observed. Factual prediction does not validate responses to unrecorded treatment alternatives.

5.3 Agent metrics and component ablation

Agent coverage is the proportion of evaluated cases with a non-abstaining output. Agreement is the proportion of non-abstaining decisions for which the selected action category matches the recorded category. Unsupported- selection rate is the proportion of selected actions that fail the behavior-support criterion q⁡(H,a)≥ηq(H,a)\geq\eta. We additionally report average calls per case. Agreement is descriptive and does not establish that recorded clinician actions are optimal. A zero unsupported-selection rate is partly enforced by the interface and is not independent evidence of clinical safety.

The component ablation compares no gate, the support gate alone, the disagreement gate alone, and the joint gate, using a common ensemble. We interpret factual risk together with agent coverage. Because the reported results are aggregate point estimates without per-seed dispersion or hospital-level uncertainty estimates, comparisons are descriptive; no statistical significance or confidence interval is inferred from the tabulated values.

6 Results

6.1 Cohort composition

The hospital-held-out test partition contains 1,880 ICU stays and 6,300 decision transitions. Its 11.0% MAP-target missingness exceeds the 9.4% observed in training. Across the three partitions, 12,500 unresolvable dose records are excluded. These counts describe record exclusions rather than additional excluded patients.

6.2 Selective prediction on unseen hospitals

Joint gating retains 62.0% of factual transitions, with MAP MAE of 7.3 mmHg and heart-rate MAE of 9.6 bpm (Table 2). Random selection at the same coverage yields errors of 9.2 mmHg and 11.6 bpm, respectively. The corresponding relative error reductions are 20.7% for MAP and 17.2% for heart rate. The matched-coverage comparison suggests that the retained transitions are more predictable than a random subset of equal size.

The support-only gate retains 77.0% of factual transitions with MAP MAE of 8.6 mmHg, whereas the disagreement-only gate retains 79.0% with MAP MAE of 7.9 mmHg. Joint gating has the lowest error but also the lowest coverage among these rules, so these unmatched-coverage comparisons should not be interpreted as isolating a predictive advantage independent of selection. Empirical coverage of nominal 90% prediction intervals is 81.5% without gating, 84.0% for support-only gating, 85.7% for disagreement-only gating, and 87.8% for joint gating. Coverage remains below the nominal 90% level for every selection rule.

6.3 Agent behavior and decision coverage

The ungated ensemble agent produces a decision in 99.5% of cases, with 55.0% agreement and a 12.0% unsupported-selection rate. SG-WM achieves 60.0% agreement at 81.0% coverage, with no unsupported selections (Table 3). Relative to the ungated agent, these values represent a 5.0 percentage-point increase in agreement, an 18.5 percentage-point reduction in coverage, and a 12.0 percentage-point reduction in unsupported selections. The lower coverage is an essential part of the result: 60.0% agreement is conditional on the 81.0% of decision cases accepted by the gate, not the entire test cohort. The comparison is therefore not a paired assessment of action selection on the same patients, and it does not establish an improvement in clinical outcomes.

Average calls per case are 4.6 for SG-WM and 4.8 for the ungated ensemble agent, a descriptive reduction of 4.2%. These aggregate call counts do not establish lower monetary cost or latency. The direct language-model baseline uses fewer calls but has lower agreement and a higher unsupported-selection rate. Behavior cloning has no unsupported selections in the reported evaluation, showing that this diagnostic alone does not distinguish the proposed agent.

6.4 Component ablation

As shown in Table 4, factual risk is 0.53 without gating, 0.50 with support-only gating, 0.46 with disagreement-only gating, and 0.43 with the joint gate. Joint gating reduces reported risk by 0.10, or 18.9%, relative to the ungated interface. Its agent coverage is 81.0%, compared with 93.0% for support-only and 90.0% for disagreement-only gating. The two criteria therefore produce a stronger selection effect when combined. Because the retained cases differ, the ablation supports a risk–coverage trade-off rather than a coverage-independent claim of superiority.

7 Discussion and limitations

The results support selective use of clinical simulation: at the same 62.0% factual coverage, joint gating identifies transitions with lower MAP and heart-rate error than random selection. The interval-coverage increase is consistent with a more predictable retained subset, although undercoverage remains. Combining action support and ensemble disagreement also yields lower factual risk than either criterion alone, at the cost of more abstention.

Agent decision coverage is higher than factual gate coverage because an agent can choose among several proposed candidates, whereas factual evaluation applies the gate to the single recorded action. The 81.0% agent coverage therefore does not conflict with 62.0% factual coverage. At the same time, higher action agreement on accepted cases cannot establish improved treatment selection for the full population. Unsupported-selection rates measure a property targeted by the gate and must be interpreted with that construction in mind.

The analysis has several limitations. Aggregate estimates do not quantify sampling variability, seed-to-seed variation, or hospital-specific performance. An ensemble may agree while being systematically wrong, and a behavior model may reproduce biased historical practice. Selective rejection can disproportionately affect patients with sparse monitoring or unusual treatment histories; subgroup error and coverage are needed to characterize this risk.

The index-dose formulation simplifies a continuously changing treatment process. Delayed documentation, concurrent drugs, fluids, severity, and clinician judgment can confound associations between dose and future physiology. Dose binning discards detail. The small number of documented zero-dose transitions further limits evidence about withholding or discontinuing norepinephrine. Excluding unresolvable records narrows the represented population, and hospital-held-out evaluation does not address all temporal or geographic shifts. These findings concern retrospective factual prediction and interface behavior rather than causal treatment effects, mortality benefit, or prospective safety.

8 Conclusion

SG-WM combines observational action support and ensemble disagreement to regulate a clinical agent’s access to simulated patient responses. On held-out eICU hospitals, the joint gate yields a MAP MAE of 7.3 mmHg at 62.0% factual coverage, compared with 9.2 mmHg for matched random selection. The gated agent achieves 60.0% recorded-action agreement at 81.0% decision coverage, while enforcing its support constraint. The main empirical finding is a measurable reliability–coverage trade-off, motivating validation of selective simulation interfaces before their use in clinical decision support.

Appendix A Implementation and calibration protocol

Table 5 summarizes the dynamics ensemble, agent, and validation-only gate configuration.

Dataset partition and preprocessing.

The development protocol partitions 70 hospitals into 42 training, 14 validation, and 14 test sites. The respective patient counts are 5,200, 1,650, and 1,800; eligible ICU-stay counts are 5,400, 1,730, and 1,880; and decision-transition counts are 18,500, 5,900, and 6,300. The partitions contain 210, 65, and 70 documented zero-dose transitions, respectively. MAP-target missingness is 9.4%, 10.1%, and 11.0%. Dose-record exclusions caused by unresolvable concentration, weight, or units number 7,300, 2,400, and 2,800 records, for a total of 12,500. These exclusions are record-level counts, not patient exclusions. Action bin cutpoints and feature scaling are derived exclusively from training data.

Validation and test isolation.

Support scores are estimated from past observations and the candidate action; disagreement is computed from the three dynamic-model means. Starting from η0\eta_{0} and τ0\tau_{0}, quantile-based calibration and grid search on validation sites yield η∗=0.06\eta^{*}=0.06 and τ∗=0.025\tau^{*}=0.025. The resulting pair is locked for all test-hospital analyses, including the support-only, disagreement-only, and joint-gate assessments. Neither test outcomes nor future clinical measurements enter candidate generation, scaling, or threshold selection.

Appendix B Time alignment and dose representation

The modeling unit is a patient-history–action pair. For a decision boundary tt, HtH_{t} contains historical observations available before the boundary; the action input is the first interpretable documented norepinephrine rate in (t,t+30 min](t,t+30\text{ min}]. The future physiological target is summarized over (t+180,t+240 min](t+180,t+240\text{ min}]. This separation prevents the target window from entering the pre-decision representation.

An explicit zero rate is distinct from missing documentation. Dose conversion requires interpretable units and, where needed, a valid weight or drug concentration. For μ\mug/min records, the weight-normalized dose is the rate divided by weight in kg. For mL/h records, a verified concentration is necessary before normalizing the dose. Unresolvable records are excluded.

Appendix C Model outputs and uncertainty decomposition

Each dynamics model predicts a mean μm​j\mu_{mj} and variance σm​j2\sigma^{2}_{mj} for physiological target jj. The moment-matched ensemble variance is

vj​(H,a)=1M​∑m=1M[σm​j2​(H,a)+μm​j​(H,a)2]−μ¯j​(H,a)2.v_{j}(H,a)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\left[\sigma^{2}_{mj}(H,a)+\mu_{mj}(H,a)^{2}\right]-\bar{\mu}_{j}(H,a)^{2}. (8)

The within-model variance and between-model disagreement capture different sources of predictive spread. The gate uses between-model disagreement, while prediction intervals use the ensemble predictive distribution. Both quantities concern the observational model and do not identify uncertainty in a causal treatment effect.

Appendix D Candidate eligibility and abstention

For a candidate set 𝒞t\mathcal{C}_{t}, let

𝒞t+={a∈𝒞t:q(Ht,a)≥η,u(Ht,a)≤τ}.\mathcal{C}^{+}_{t}=\{a\in\mathcal{C}_{t}:q(H_{t},a)\geq\eta,\ u(H_{t},a)\leq\tau\}. (9)

If 𝒞t+\mathcal{C}^{+}_{t} is empty, the output is abstention. Otherwise, the agent refines its choice using released candidate summaries and a validator restricts its final selection to 𝒞t+\mathcal{C}^{+}_{t}. Rejected candidates carry support or disagreement reason codes instead of numerical response forecasts. This design keeps a rejected prediction from being reused as if it were accepted evidence.

Appendix E Interpretation of evaluation metrics

Factual-transition coverage applies to the recorded action; decision coverage applies to the existence and selection of an eligible candidate. These denominators are distinct. Agreement is conditional on a non-abstaining decision and therefore depends on selection. A comparison at different coverage levels is not a paired comparison on an identical patient subset.

Relative error reductions in the main text are calculated from the reported point estimates. The MAP comparison is (9.2−7.3)/9.2=20.7%(9.2-7.3)/9.2=20.7\%, and the heart-rate comparison is (11.6−9.6)/11.6=17.2%(11.6-9.6)/11.6=17.2\%. The ablation risk reduction is (0.53−0.43)/0.53=18.9%(0.53-0.43)/0.53=18.9\%. The difference in agreement between the gated and ungated agents is 5.0 percentage points, rather than 5.0% relative improvement. These calculations do not imply statistical significance.

Appendix F Prediction intervals

The interval metric is empirical coverage of nominal 90% prediction intervals. The reported 87.8% coverage for the joint gate remains below the nominal 90% level. Since interval widths and conditional coverage estimates are not included in the comparison, the increase in empirical coverage alone does not establish well-calibrated or equally informative intervals across subsets.
